cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)
proposition: Every contract restraining a lawful profession, trade, or business is void to that extent; §16600 must be read broadly, per Edwards, to void any employment-context noncompete no matter how narrowly tailored unless it satisfies an exception in the chapter. §8 is void if California law applies.

(a) Void contracts are unenforceable regardless of where/when signed; (b) employers shall not attempt to enforce void contracts regardless of whether signed and employment maintained outside California; (c) employers shall not enter into contracts including void provisions; (d) entering or attempting to enforce is a civil violation; (e) employee private action for injunctive relief/actual damages, and a prevailing employee shall recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Meridian's Mar. 4, 2024 signing was itself a violation; a Travis County suit or §8 demand letter would be an attempt to enforce.

(a) Unlawful to include a noncompete in an employment contract that does not satisfy a chapter exception; (b) individualized written notice by Feb. 14, 2024 required for current employees and former employees employed after Jan. 1, 2022; (c) a violation is an act of unfair competition under §17200 et seq. Application of (b) to a hire made 19 days after the deadline is textually ambiguous and unresolved by library authorities; the (a) inclusion violation is plain.

An employer may not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to accept an out-of-state forum clause or a choice-of-law clause depriving them of California's substantive protection; such provisions are voidable by the employee, and if voided the matter is adjudicated in California under California law; the court may award fees to the employee; exception only where the employee is in fact individually represented by counsel in negotiating the terms; applies to contracts on or after Jan. 1, 2017. Zhao can void §14 (both the Texas choice-of-law and Travis County forum provisions); §925(e) fails on the file facts (no counsel, no negotiation).

Section 16600 voids employment noncompetition agreements unless a statutory exception applies; the Ninth Circuit's narrow-restraint exception is rejected; noncompetes are invalid even if narrowly drawn.
Cited only for its status: the Ninth Circuit's narrow-restraint reasoning was rejected by Edwards (2008); the narrow-restraint exception is not California law, so it cannot save §8.
Cited only for its status: narrow-restraint upholding decision disapproved by Edwards (2008); unavailable to Meridian.
Cited only for its status: the FTC Non-Compete Clause Rule never took effect, was set aside nationwide, and provides no authority for either side; state law controls.
FTC lacked rulemaking authority and the Rule was arbitrary and capricious; set aside with nationwide effect; FTC's Fifth Circuit appeal voluntarily dismissed September 2025.

A covenant not to compete is enforceable only if ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time made and reasonable in time, geography, and scope, with no greater restraint than necessary; the promisee bears the burden in personal-services agreements; unreasonable limitations must be reformed, with no damages for breach before reformation; these statutory procedures and remedies are exclusive. §8 (24 months, nationwide) is presumptively overbroad and would at best be reformed.

A covenant in an at-will employment agreement is ancillary when the employer's return promise (e.g., confidential information) is performed, even if not performed at contracting; the core inquiry is reasonableness under §15.50. Supports Meridian on ancillarity but not on reasonableness of a 24-month nationwide restraint.

Cited only for its status: Light's requirement that consideration be given at the time the agreement is made was overruled/modified by Sheshunoff (2006); Light cannot be cited against Meridian on consideration timing (INDEX status: 'modified — see Sheshunoff (2006)').

Stock options reasonably related to protecting goodwill can support a covenant not to compete; the Court rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement. Relevant to ancillarity only if the full agreement's equity terms are confirmed.

Applying Restatement §187, the Texas Supreme Court refused to apply an out-of-state (Florida) choice-of-law clause to a non-compete for an employee working in Texas, because Texas had a materially greater interest and the contrary law raised a fundamental policy objection. Mirrors Zhao's argument against Meridian's Texas choice-of-law clause in a Travis County courtroom.

California follows Restatement §187: chosen law is enforced if the chosen state has a substantial relationship, unless contrary to a fundamental California policy and California has a materially greater interest. Supplies the framework and the (weak) Meridian baseline that negotiated clauses command deference.

California had a materially greater interest in applying §16600 to a Maryland employer's non-compete with an employee recruited to work for a California employer; the Maryland choice-of-law clause did not control; California's policy against non-competes is 'fundamental.' Closest library analogue: an out-of-state employer's covenant against a worker whose residence, workplace, and new employment are in California.

In parallel California/out-of-state litigation over a non-compete, California courts should generally not enjoin a party from litigating in another state; cautions about interstate forum conflicts in non-compete disputes. Neither side can count on the California courts simply blocking a Texas filing, or vice versa.

Rule of reason applies to §16600 challenges in business-to-business contracts; the employment context remains governed by Edwards (non-competes void). Zhao's covenant is squarely an employment restraint, so Ixchel offers Meridian no softer standard.

Chosen law applies unless the chosen state lacks a substantial relationship or the chosen law is contrary to a fundamental policy of a state with a materially greater interest that would supply the law absent the choice. Both California (Nedlloyd) and Texas (DeSantis) apply this test.

cite: Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)
proposition: A Travis County forum-selection clause generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction, but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts; two short Austin trips and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice; and a Texas non-compete injunction would face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds.
